name: Hydroxyapatite (toothpaste)
lead: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste contains synthetic hydroxyapatite, the calcium phosphate mineral that makes up most of tooth enamel, in micro- or nano-sized crystals. It is marketed as a fluoride-free alternative for protecting and remineralising enamel.[1][2][23] The appeal for appearance is a smoother, stronger-feeling and less sensitive tooth surface, fewer early enamel lesions and, in the way products are marketed, whiter-looking teeth through surface-stain removal and repair of microscopic roughness.[9][8][23]

People use it as a daily toothpaste in place of, or sometimes alongside, a fluoride product, and brands also sell it in mouthwashes, gels and whitening kits.[23][25] It has a long history in Japan, where it was launched in 1980, and has spread to Europe and the United States through social media and brand marketing.[26][25]

An 18-month randomized trial in adults found a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste not inferior to a 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste for preventing new caries, and a 24-month trial in children reported results favouring hydroxyapatite-fluoride toothpastes on active enamel lesions.[6][5] Fluoride remains the long-established standard in caries prevention, and the American Dental Association has said evidence on hydroxyapatite's clinical effectiveness remains limited and ambiguous.[3][25]
infobox: Enamel remineralisation, caries prevention, sensitivity relief, surface whitening[1][9][23]
Nano form: up to 29.5 percent in toothpaste for rod-shaped particles (SCCS, 2025)[27]

paras: NASA's Spinoff magazine traces the idea to the 1960s, when NASA Electronics Research Center scientist Bernard Rubin, noticing parallels between crystal growth in gel and bone mineralisation, helped patent a method for growing crystals that would convert to hydroxyapatite on a damaged tooth, granted in 1972.[26] Shuji Sakuma founded Sangi Co. Ltd. in Tokyo in 1974, acquired the patent after visiting Rubin, and proposed a toothpaste infused directly with hydroxyapatite.[26]

Sangi launched Apadent in Japan in 1980 and Apagard in 1985; because approval for medical claims took years, early products were sold as whitening beauty toothpastes, and Japan recognised hydroxyapatite as an anti-cavity agent in 1993, according to NASA's account.[26] Sangi reports having sold over 160 million tubes.[26] The company-sourced history means exact dates should be treated as the company's account. In the United States the FDA does not allow cavity-prevention claims for non-fluoride toothpastes, so products there are commonly sold on sensitivity relief, whitening and enamel-care claims.[26][25]

Tooth enamel is largely hydroxyapatite. Once formed, it cannot be biologically repaired by the body, and saliva supplies calcium, phosphate and fluoride ions that support remineralisation of demineralised surfaces [4]. Hydroxyapatite toothpastes add particles intended to deposit directly on enamel and fill in lesions, a mechanism examined in laboratory, in situ and clinical studies [1][2]. Nano-hydroxyapatite is also studied outside dentistry as a bone graft and scaffold material, a separate field [12][7].

Wikipedia reports that hydroxyapatite makes up about 70 to 80 percent of the mass of enamel and dentin, that demineralisation removes calcium and phosphate from the crystals and remineralisation restores them, and that with fluoride present the mineral can become fluorapatite, which is more acid-resistant.[23] Nano-hydroxyapatite products are described as sealing exposed dentinal tubules and as possibly reducing biofilm formation on enamel in laboratory studies.[23] Some commentators describe the effect as a surface layer; a dentist reviewing the field on a practice website says that layer can be brushed or dissolved off, an attributed view rather than a trial result.[25] Hydroxyapatite particles can also be shaped as rods or needles, a distinction that matters for the EU's safety rules.[27]

Caries prevention. An 18-month double-blind trial of 189 adults compared a fluoride-free hydroxyapatite toothpaste with 1450 ppm fluoride toothpaste; 89.3% of the hydroxyapatite group and 87.4% of the fluoride group showed no increase in DMFS, and the authors concluded non-inferiority [6]. A triple-blind trial in 610 young children tested hydroxyapatite-fluoride toothpastes against fluoride toothpastes over 24 months and reported a statistically significant reduction in enamel lesions in the hydroxyapatite-fluoride group [5]. A scoping review of nano-hydroxyapatite in early caries mapped the literature on remineralisation of early lesions [2], and a narrative review summarised in vitro, in situ and in vivo findings [1].

Sensitivity and whitening. A double-blind randomized trial of 105 people found a fluoride-free nano-hydroxyapatite gel toothpaste produced lower dentin hypersensitivity scores at 2 and 4 weeks than fluoride or placebo [9]. In a 60-person bleaching trial, 6% hydrogen peroxide with 2% nano-hydroxyapatite produced comparable shade change to peroxide alone, with significantly less sensitivity; shade partly relapsed by 9 months in both groups [8]. Other trials examined it with ozone on early approximal caries [10] and on erosive lesions caused by orange juice [11]. Evidence that hydroxyapatite toothpaste whitens teeth on its own is not found in these sources.

Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of hydroxyapatite oral-care products and caries were published in 2021 and updated in 2024, and a 2019 network meta-analysis of non-restorative caries treatments covered 44 trials with 7,378 participants.[28][29][30] NPR reports that a 2021 study of 177 children for almost a year and the 2023 trial of 171 young adults found results similar to fluoride, that both were funded by the German Dr. Wolff Group (which owns two hydroxyapatite toothpaste brands), and that a 2019 trial in 133 higher-risk people over about five months also found similar performance.[25] Bennett Amaechi was quoted there saying it is as effective as fluoride for remineralisation, while Livia Tenuta said there are very few studies, recruiting people at low caries risk, and that she recommends fluoride toothpaste.[25]

Fluoride is described as a cornerstone of caries prevention through enamel remineralisation, inhibition of demineralisation and antibacterial activity, although controversies persist over systemic exposure and community water fluoridation [3]. Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is presented by reviewers as a fluoride-free option under investigation, and trials so far have mostly compared it with fluoride products rather than with no treatment [1][6]. Longer trials in more diverse populations have not been published.

The cited trials report it as safe and well tolerated; the authors of the adult trial concluded it was a safe and efficient anticaries agent [6]. Regulatory status of specific products varies by country and is not addressed in the cited studies.

The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) reviewed nano-hydroxyapatite in cosmetics. Its 2021 opinion said it could not conclude on the safety of the rod-shaped form in oral-care products because genotoxicity concerns were not excluded, and it said needle-shaped particles should not be used in cosmetic products.[27] Later opinions, reported by law-firm summaries and Wikipedia, cleared rod-shaped particles meeting defined shape and surface criteria, and a July 2025 final opinion considered it safe up to 29.5 percent in toothpaste and 10 percent in mouthwash, not applicable to needle-shaped material.[23][31]

Dentist Jin-Ho Phark told NPR that patients ask about hydroxyapatite after seeing it on social media, where influencers promote it quite intensively, and that interest has grown alongside fluoride scepticism linked in the article to US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.'s criticism of fluoridation.[25] The ADA acknowledges growing use and some evidence of remineralisation but spokesperson Ada Cooper said clinical effectiveness evidence remains limited and ambiguous; the ADA recommends fluoride toothpaste, and only fluoride toothpastes carry its Seal of Acceptance, according to a consumer summary.[25][32] The products are often more expensive than conventional pastes.[25]

On looksmax.org, hydroxyapatite appears in two unrelated contexts: a thread on how safe fluoride in toothpaste is, where one poster says dentists dissuade patients from fluoride-free pastes, and a discussion of hydroxyapatite implants for facial augmentation, a separate surgical material.[33][34]

timeline.event: US patent for growing crystals that convert to hydroxyapatite on teeth, from NASA scientists, granted.[26]
Sangi Co. founded in Tokyo; acquires the patent.[26]
Sangi launches Apadent hydroxyapatite toothpaste in Japan.[26]
Japan recognises hydroxyapatite as an anti-cavity agent.[26]
Trial of bleaching with and without nano-hydroxyapatite reports reduced sensitivity.[8]
Randomized trial finds nano-hydroxyapatite toothpaste reduces dentin hypersensitivity.[9]
EU SCCS cannot conclude on safety of rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite in oral care; a 2021 meta-analysis of caries prevention is published.[27][29]
18-month trial finds hydroxyapatite toothpaste non-inferior to fluoride in adults.[6]
24-month trial in children reports effects on active enamel lesions; SCCS final opinion sets limits for rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite.[5][31]

lore.intro: Hydroxyapatite toothpaste is discussed mainly on social media and in dental commentary as a fluoride-free option; on looksmax.org fluoride is debated as a general oral-health question.[25][33]

claims.claim: Hydroxyapatite is as good as fluoride at preventing cavities
claims.believers: Brands and some researchers cite trials showing non-inferiority to fluoride in adults and similar outcomes in children.[6][25]
claims.experts: The ADA calls the clinical evidence limited and ambiguous, and one expert noted few studies and low-risk participants; some trials were funded by a hydroxyapatite manufacturer.[25]

claims.believers: Products are marketed for whitening and Apagard was first sold in Japan as a whitening toothpaste.[26]
claims.experts: Trials in the reviewed literature tested sensitivity with peroxide bleaching rather than whitening by the paste alone.[8]

claims.believers: Users describe less sensitivity, especially during bleaching.[8]
claims.experts: A 2018 randomized trial of 105 people found lower hypersensitivity scores at 2 and 4 weeks versus fluoride or placebo, and Wikipedia reports a 2019 meta-analysis with similar findings for some stimuli.[9][23]

claims.believers: Fluoride-sceptical communities favour hydroxyapatite as a way to avoid fluoride.[25]
claims.experts: Health experts quoted by NPR say low fluoride levels are safe and beneficial, and that studies linking fluoride to lower IQ examined levels above those recommended in US water.[25]

claims.believers: Wikipedia notes hydroxyapatite is the same mineral as most of enamel and is widely used in dentistry and oral surgery.[23]
claims.experts: The EU SCCS said in 2021 it could not conclude on safety of rod-shaped nano-hydroxyapatite in oral care and warned against needle-shaped particles, before later opinions set conditions and concentration limits.[27][31]

card.summary: A fluoride-free remineralising toothpaste built on enamel's own mineral; one 18-month adult trial matched fluoride for caries, whitening claims are thin.
card.note: Trials mostly compare with fluoride; evidence for whitening on its own was not found.

quick.overview:
Hydroxyapatite toothpaste uses the same mineral that makes up tooth enamel, in tiny particles, as a fluoride-free way to protect and remineralise teeth.

An 18-month adult trial found it not inferior to fluoride at preventing new cavities, and a child trial and small sensitivity trials have also been positive. Evidence that it whitens teeth by itself was not found.
quick.mechanism: Particles are meant to deposit on enamel and fill microscopic defects in demineralised areas, supported by saliva's calcium and phosphate. In bleaching trials it reduced sensitivity when added to peroxide.
quick.risks: Trials report no safety concerns, and the main safety debate in the field concerns fluoride rather than hydroxyapatite. Long-term, large-scale data are still limited.
